analysis.one_liner: Lets non-bank loan buyers keep the bank's original interest rate on loans they purchase, overriding state rate caps.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on it: the bill was referred to the Banking Committee in July 2017 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the "valid-when-made" rule into federal law: once a bank makes a loan at a rate that is legal for the bank, the rate stays legal forever, even after the loan is sold to a non-bank debt buyer or lender, and state laws that cap interest rates could not be applied to the buyer. Sponsors argued this preserves the market where banks sell loans, keeping credit flowing to borrowers. Critics said it would let payday- and high-cost-style lenders route loans through a partner bank and then sell them, escaping state interest-rate caps that states use to protect residents.
analysis.who_benefits: Non-bank buyers of consumer loans — debt buyers and fintech lenders — gain, because they could enforce a bank's interest rate on loans they purchase even in states with lower rate caps. Banks gain a bigger, safer market for selling loans. Sponsors argued borrowers with low credit scores gain by keeping credit available that a 2015 court ruling put at risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Non-bank loan buyers and fintech lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that a loan valid when made as to its maximum rate stays valid at that rate no matter to whom it is later sold, assigned, or transferred, and may be enforced by the third party "notwithstanding any State law to the contrary" [S3].
Sponsors argued the valid-when-made doctrine brings certainty to transferred loans, widens the pool of loan buyers, and lowers the cost of credit at origination [S3].
Sponsors cited a study finding that a 2015 appeals-court ruling on this issue fell hardest on low- and moderate-income borrowers with lower credit scores [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers pay. Loans sold to non-banks would carry whatever rate the bank charged, even if a state caps interest below that for everyone else. Residents of states with strict interest-rate caps, and the states themselves, lose that protection for loans sold on the secondary market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state interest-rate caps: the buyer could enforce the bank's rate "notwithstanding any State law to the contrary," so states could no longer apply their own usury limits to loans sold after origination [S3].

Consumer groups argued this is the legal basis of "rent-a-bank" lending, in which a non-bank lender originates high-cost loans through a partner bank and then sells them, letting the non-bank charge rates the state never allowed it to charge.

Once a high-rate loan is valid regardless of who holds it, a borrower could not use state law to challenge the rate even after the loan changes hands, removing a lever states and borrowers have used against debt collectors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The credit-access argument is real: if buyers cannot rely on a loan's original rate, banks may sell fewer loans and some borrowers with weak credit lose options. But the bill's remedy is sweeping — it nullifies state interest-rate caps for transferred loans nationwide rather than addressing the specific case. States have long used rate caps as their main consumer-protection tool, and this bill would let rates set through a bank partner outride those caps. A narrower bill protecting legitimate loan sales without opening the door to high-cost rent-a-bank structures was never taken up instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in July 2017 and referred to the Banking Committee, which never took it up, so the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) introduced the bill on July 27, 2017, joined by Sens. Toomey, Peters, and Daines as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S5].
That was the only action taken: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the Senate [S5].
The bill carried four cosponsors, three Republicans and one Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary borrowers and the states kept their interest-rate caps, because the bill never advanced; non-bank loan buyers lost a chance to have their ability to enforce bank rates written into law.

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.role: U.S. Senator from Virginia, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case that the valid-when-made doctrine keeps credit flowing to lower-income borrowers.

for.name: Sen. Pat Toomey, Sen. Gary Peters, and Sen. Steve Daines
Non-bank consumer lenders and debt buyers
for.role: Industry that purchases loans made by banks
for.what_they_did: Backed legislation to reverse a 2015 court ruling so they could enforce banks' interest rates on purchased loans.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote or hearing on the bill after it was referred to his committee; it sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: Consumer advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as opening the door to rent-a-bank lending that evades state interest-rate caps.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill with two other Democrats and three Republicans signed on among the sponsor and four cosponsors, so support crossed party lines; opposition never appeared on any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Non-bank loan buyers (debt buyers, fintech consumer lenders)
industries.note: The bill would let them enforce a partner bank's interest rate on purchased loans in any state, even where that rate exceeds the state's cap. Their gain comes from the higher interest borrowers pay.

industries.industry: Banks and savings institutions that sell loans
industries.note: A guaranteed rule that sold loans keep their original rate makes it safer and more valuable for banks to sell loan portfolios. Sponsors argued this also lowers borrowing costs at origination.

industries.industry: State regulators and state usury-law enforcement
industries.note: The bill says the rate can be enforced 'notwithstanding any State law to the contrary,' removing states' ability to cap rates on transferred loans.
The bill applies the same rule to federal credit union loans, adding certainty for loan sales but extending the override of state rate caps to credit-union-originated debt as well.
